hints: Notice the $1.0 \text{ kg}$ weight of about $10 \text{ N}$ still acts vertically downwards in the vacuum when the $50 \text{ N}$ upward force starts.
Connect the $50 \text{ N}$ upward force and the weight to the resultant force, then use $F = ma$ to find the upward acceleration.
Take downwards as positive with $u = +60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and use $v = u + at$ over $t = 2.0 \text{ s}$ to find the signed velocity, then take speed as its magnitude.
walkthrough: Take downwards as positive. Initial velocity is $u = +60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and time is $t = 2.0 \text{ s}$.
Weight acts downwards: $W = mg = 1.0 \times 9.81 \approx 10 \text{ N}$. The extra $50 \text{ N}$ acts upwards, so resultant force is $F = 50 - 10 = 40 \text{ N}$ upwards.
Use $F = ma$ for magnitude: $a = F/m = 40/1.0 = 40 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards, so in the downwards-positive sign convention $a = -40 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Use $v = u + at = 60 + (-40) \times 2.0 = 60 - 80 = -20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. The negative sign means $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ upwards.
Speed is the magnitude, $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. This is option A.

options.A: Net upward force of $40 \text{ N}$ gives $40 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ upward acceleration, reducing the $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ downward speed to $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ after $2.0 \text{ s}$.
options.B: This results from using only the $50 \text{ N}$ force to find acceleration and ignoring the $10 \text{ N}$ weight acting downwards.
options.C: This adds the change in velocity to the initial speed instead of subtracting it for an upward net force opposing downward motion.
options.D: This adds $g t$ to the initial speed as if the object continued in free fall with no $50 \text{ N}$ upward force.
